raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old male with a longstanding history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c of 13%) was admitted to our hospital with a complaint of right frontal headache and vomiting for 5 days. The initial laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count, renal, and hepatic profiles but elevated glucose level (24.4 mmol/L). His blood culture and HIV serology were negative and the CD4 count was normal. The initial brain CT scan showed circumferential mucosal thickening in the sphenoid sinuses, which was more on the right side, and mild scattered mucosal thickening in the other paranasal sinuses. In addition, there was fluid opacification of the mastoid air cells and middle ear cavities. The patient was started on insulin and Augmentin intravenously.
Five days later, the patient complained of sudden loss of vision in the right eye and jaw pain. The brain CT scan was repeated, and it showed progression of the inflammatory changes in the paranasal sinuses without acute brain insult. Giant cell arteritis was suspected and treatment with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gm daily was initiated. Temporal artery biopsy was performed 2 days later and found to be normal, and corticosteroids were discontinued. However, the patient's symptoms worsened, and thus a third CT scan brain was obtained, which showed progression of the sinusitis to the retropharyngeal abscess. A sinonasal biopsy was obtained, and its histopathological examination showed positive GMS stain for fungus, suggestive of mucormycosis [Figure 1]. The patient was then treated with amphotericin B. A week later, the patient developed sepsis, and thus was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin and meropenem. The chest and abdominal CT scan showed mild bilateral pleural effusions and mucosal edema involving the ascending colon without obstruction or significant lymphadenopathy.
Two weeks after his admission, he developed melena mixed with streaks of blood and his hemoglobin dropped from 83 to 75 g/L. Subsequently, the patient underwent an upper GI endoscopy and sigmoidoscopy. The upper GI endoscopy revealed severe erythematous gastritis and a huge gastric ulcer covered by necrotic-looking tissues with non-bleeding visible vessel, which was clipped [Figure 2]. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the edges of the ulcer. Sigmoidoscopy revealed pale mucosa, with ischemic changes 18-25 cm from the anal verge [Figure 3], following which biopsies were obtained.
Microscopic examination of the gastric mucosa demonstrated severe acute chronic inflammation, fibrinous exudate, and extensive ulceration. In the rectal mucosa, numerous fibrin microthrombi were also identified. Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) special stains demonstrated numerous fungal microorganisms in the form of single and clustered small (2-10 mum) narrow-based budding yeasts in ulcerated gastric and rectal mucosa, suggestive of cryptococcus species [Figure 4a and b]. Specific stains such as Fontana-Masson or mucicarmine stain were not available, and the tissues were not sent for microbiological cultures. The immunohistochemical staining for cytomegalovirus was negative. Despite the early diagnosis and appropriate treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics and an antifungal agent, the patients' condition deteriorated with refractory septic shock and multiorgan failure, and unfortunately, he passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 13%) presented with a 5-day history of right frontal headache and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 5 days of right frontal headache and vomiting alongside severe hyperglycemia (24.4 mmol/L) and sphenoid sinusitis. Five days after admission, he developed sudden right-eye blindness and jaw pain, followed by retropharyngeal abscess extension, sepsis, and (at 2 weeks) melena with hematochezia from a massive necrotic gastric ulcer and ischemic proctocolitis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right frontal headache, vomiting, and subsequent sudden right eye vision loss, jaw pain, sepsis, and melena with blood streaks.

objective.physical_examination: Developed sudden complete visual loss in the right eye and jaw pain on hospital day 5, sepsis at week 1, and melena mixed with blood streaks at week 2, progressing to refractory septic shock and multiorgan failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood glucose 24.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 13%, normal initial CBC, renal, and hepatic profiles (hemoglobin later dropped from 83 g/L to 75 g/L during GI bleeding at week 2), and negative blood cultures and HIV serology.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was normal. Serial head/sinus CTs showed right-predominant sphenoid and pan-sinus mucosal thickening with mastoid/middle ear opacification progressing to a retropharyngeal abscess without acute brain parenchymal insult; temporal artery biopsy was normal; sinonasal biopsy GMS stain was positive for fungal elements initially thought to suggest mucormycosis. Chest and abdominal CT showed mild bilateral pleural effusions and ascending colon mucosal edema. Week 2 upper GI endoscopy and sigmoidoscopy revealed severe erythematous gastritis, a huge necrotic gastric ulcer with a visible vessel (clipped), and pale ischemic rectal mucosa (18-25 cm from anal verge); gastric and rectal mucosal biopsies demonstrated ulceration, fibrin microthrombi, negative CMV immunohistochemistry, and numerous single and clustered small (2-10 um) narrow-based budding yeasts on PAS and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stains consistent with Cryptococcus species.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of fatal invasive gastrointestinal (gastric ulcer and ischemic rectal) and sinonasal/retropharyngeal cryptococcosis in an HIV-negative patient with severely uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 13%), confirmed by sinonasal, gastric ulcer, and rectal mucosal biopsy histopathology using periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stains demonstrating 2-10 um narrow-based budding yeasts (with giant cell arteritis and CMV excluded by temporal artery biopsy and immunohistochemistry). Treated with insulin, endoscopic hemoclipping, broad-spectrum antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate, escalated to vancomycin and meropenem), and IV amphotericin B, but the patient died of refractory septic shock and multiorgan failure.
